headline: An ANU Thesis Argues Consciousness Is the Optimal Learning Strategy
lede: Michael Timothy Bennett, a doctoral candidate at the Australian National University, has published a thesis arguing that consciousness is not an evolutionary accident but the mathematically optimal solution to the problem of learning in an uncertain world. The 2025 work, *How to Build Conscious Machines*, draws on algorithmic information theory, philosophy of biology, and cognitive science to propose that *valence* — the primitive attraction or repulsion present even in single-celled life — scales up into the full machinery of human self-awareness. The argument, if it holds, would make the *philosophical zombie* computationally impossible and place current large language models categorically outside the bounds of consciousness.
body:
The thesis's mathematical core challenges a foundational assumption of most machine learning: that the shortest hypothesis consistent with the data generalizes best. This principle — formalized in *Solomonoff induction* and measured by *Kolmogorov complexity*, the length of the minimal program needed to reproduce an output — underlies Bayesian inference and the intuition that models should be regularized toward simplicity. Bennett argues the target should instead be the **weakest** hypothesis: the one consistent with the greatest number of possible worlds. He calls optimizing for this property *w-maxing*, and reports that choosing weak constraints over compressed ones yielded a 110–500% improvement in generalization on binary arithmetic tasks, a result formalized in a companion paper accepted to the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 2025. The competing approaches — which he terms *simp-maxing* (compression) and scale-maxing (more compute and data) — are, he argues, optimizing the wrong quantity, including the *free energy principle*, the influential account of brain function as prediction-error minimization.

Consciousness enters through *valence* — the irreducible quality of attraction and repulsion that even a bacterium expresses toward chemical gradients. As biological systems complexify, Bennett argues, they build *tapestries of valence*: layered, orchestrated responses across many cells that classify stimuli by their causal significance for survival. These tapestries are not a metaphor for *qualia* — the subjective texture of experience, the redness of red, the ache of cold — they are what qualia are. The move makes the *philosophical zombie* computationally impossible: a being behaviorally identical to a conscious human but lacking inner experience could not, on this account, perform the causal, self-preserving reasoning that human behavior requires. Consciousness is not decorative; it is load-bearing.

Bennett organizes consciousness into five stages: hardwired organisms with no learning (protozoa), adaptive learners without self-models (nematodes), first-order phenomenal selves (houseflies), second-order minds capable of attributing mental states to others (cats, ravens), and third-order meta-aware consciousness (humans). Current large language models fail even the first stage: they lack *reafference* — a model distinguishing world-changes they caused from those they merely observed — and their processing is, he writes, "smeared across time" rather than temporally integrated. The framework situates clearly against rivals: **Integrated Information Theory**, which defines consciousness as the amount of irreducible information a system integrates (measured as Φ), captures roughly the right intuition but ignores adaptive motivation; *Higher-Order Thought* theory, the account in which a mental state is conscious when accompanied by a representation of itself, is the closest structural relative, and Bennett's valence account provides the grounding it leaves unexplained.

The thesis has won multiple Best Student Paper awards at the Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) conference series and attracted co-authors including researchers at University College London. A Hacker News thread on the preprint generated substantive debate: critics argued the framework recycled Chalmers and Dennett without sufficient formal novelty; supporters called the w-maxing result and the valence hierarchy genuine contributions. Bennett is supervised by Yoshihiro Maruyama at ANU, whose research spans category theory, formal logic, and AI foundations. The full thesis is freely available at the ANU Open Research Repository.

concepts.definition: Bennett's proposed optimization principle: prefer the hypothesis consistent with the greatest number of possible worlds, rather than the shortest. He argues this generalizes better than compression-based approaches and reports large empirical gains on benchmark tasks. It directly contests the Occam's razor intuition that underlies most of machine learning.

Bennett's term for the dominant machine learning strategy: optimizing for the simplest, most compressed hypothesis. Rooted in Kolmogorov complexity and Bayesian inference, it underlies most regularization techniques. Bennett argues it is the wrong target for genuine generalization and that the free energy principle commits the same error.

A mathematical framework for universal prediction that defines the optimal hypothesis as the shortest program consistent with observed data. It provides the theoretical foundation for algorithmic information theory and formal Bayesian machine learning. Named after Ray Solomonoff, it is the rigorous statement of Occam's razor that Bennett directly contests.

The length of the shortest computer program that produces a given string or dataset. Used as a formal measure of a hypothesis's simplicity and as the standard proxy for generalizability in algorithmic information theory. Central to the simp-maxing paradigm Bennett argues against.

In Bennett's framework, the primitive good/bad or attract/repel quality present in any adaptive system — from bacteria responding to nutrients to humans feeling pleasure or pain. He treats valence as primary, not derived from neural mechanisms, and argues it is the foundational unit from which all consciousness is built up.

Bennett's term for the layered, multi-scale cellular responses through which complex organisms classify stimuli by their survival significance. He argues that these orchestrated signals — not some further emergent property on top of them — are what qualia physically are.

The subjective, qualitative character of experience: what it is like to see red, feel cold, or hear a note. Qualia are the core puzzle of philosophy of mind. Explaining why any physical process gives rise to subjective experience at all is called the 'hard problem of consciousness,' coined by philosopher David Chalmers.

A thought experiment: a being physically and behaviorally identical to a conscious human but entirely lacking inner experience. Philosophers use it to argue that consciousness cannot be fully reduced to physical function. Bennett argues such beings are not merely implausible but computationally ruled out by his framework.

A system's internal model that tracks which sensory changes were caused by its own actions, as distinct from externally caused changes. Key to embodied cognition and motor control. Bennett treats the absence of reafference as a core reason current large language models cannot be conscious: they cannot distinguish outputs they generated from training data they observed.

A theory of consciousness developed by Giulio Tononi that defines consciousness as proportional to Φ (phi): a measure of integrated information that cannot be decomposed into independent parts. Influential but controversial — critics note it can assign high consciousness to simple logical circuits that intuitively seem non-conscious.

An account of brain function developed by Karl Friston: the brain minimizes 'free energy' (a proxy for surprise or prediction error) by building and updating an internal generative model of the world. Highly influential in theoretical neuroscience. Bennett classifies it as a form of simp-maxing, arguing it optimizes the wrong quantity.

The philosophical view that a mental state is conscious when it is accompanied by a higher-order mental representation of that state — the mind being aware of its own awareness. Developed principally by David Rosenthal. Bennett treats it as the closest structural predecessor to his own framework, supplying valence as the grounding HOT leaves unexplained.

The hypothetical development of machine intelligence capable of performing any intellectual task a human can across arbitrary domains, as opposed to narrow AI systems optimized for specific tasks. Distinct from current large language models, which excel at language generation but lack the open-ended, embodied adaptation AGI implies.

fact_check: The 110–500% improvement in generalization cited in the text derives from Bennett's own controlled experiments on binary arithmetic tasks and has not been independently replicated. The Artificial General Intelligence conference, while a legitimate peer-reviewed Springer venue, is a specialist series; the core w-maxing result has not yet appeared in top-tier machine learning venues such as NeurIPS, ICML, or ICLR. The thesis is a preprint under review as of 2025, meaning its claims have not passed full doctoral examination. The philosophical zombie impossibility argument is a logical consequence of Bennett's framework, not an independently falsifiable empirical prediction — readers should treat it as a philosophical claim supported by the framework's premises, not a separately proven result.
